title: Design Patterns Overview
summary: Named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems. Learn the GoF categories so later deep-dive topics have a map to fit into.

blocks.markdown:
A **design pattern** is a reusable solution to a recurring design problem — not code you copy, but a proven **shape** you adapt.

- Patterns give a shared **vocabulary**: "use a Factory here" says more than a paragraph.
- They're battle-tested — someone already found the trade-offs.
- The classic catalog is the **Gang of Four (GoF)**, 23 patterns in 3 categories.
- A pattern is a **template for a solution**, applied afresh to your own classes each time.

blocks.subTitle: The three categories
blocks.markdown:
GoF splits its 23 patterns by what problem they solve.

| Category | Solves | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Creational | How objects get created | Factory, Singleton, Builder |
| Structural | How objects compose | Adapter, Decorator, Facade |
| Behavioral | How objects interact | Observer, Strategy, Command |

Deep dives on each category are separate topics.

Patterns aren't invented — they're **mined**. Someone noticed the same clean solution appearing again and again across unrelated codebases and gave it a name.

- **Shared vocabulary** — a team says "Observer" instead of re-explaining the wiring each time.
- **Proven trade-offs** — the pitfalls of a pattern are already known, so you inherit the fix, not just the idea.
- They speed up **design conversations**, not typing speed.

The **Gang of Four (GoF)** is the nickname for four authors — Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides — who wrote *Design Patterns* (1994).

- Cataloged **23 patterns** seen repeatedly in object-oriented systems.
- Organized them by **category** (creational, structural, behavioral) and by **scope** (class vs object).
- Not the only patterns that exist, but the common reference point interviewers and teams assume you know.

**Creational** patterns control **how objects get created**, hiding the messy `new` logic from the caller.

- **Factory Method** — subclass decides which class to instantiate.
- **Abstract Factory** — creates families of related objects together.
- **Builder** — assembles a complex object step by step.
- **Singleton** — guarantees exactly one instance.
- **Prototype** — creates new objects by cloning an existing one.

Deep dive: [creational-patterns](creational-patterns).

**Structural** patterns control **how objects and classes compose** into larger structures without becoming fragile.

- **Adapter** — makes one interface look like another the caller expects.
- **Decorator** — adds behavior to an object at runtime without subclassing.
- **Facade** — offers one simple interface over a complex subsystem.
- **Composite** — treats a tree of objects and single objects uniformly.
- **Proxy** — a stand-in that controls access to the real object.

Deep dive: [structural-patterns](structural-patterns).

**Behavioral** patterns control **how objects interact and share responsibility** for a task.

- **Observer** — subscribers get notified when a subject changes.
- **Strategy** — swap an algorithm at runtime behind one interface.
- **Command** — wraps a request as an object you can queue or undo.
- **State** — an object changes behavior as its internal state changes.
- **Template Method**, **Iterator**, **Chain of Responsibility**, and more round out the set.

Deep dive: [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i).

Ask what's actually hard about your problem first.

The category names describe the **question**, not the code — start there, then pick the specific pattern.

Same idea, opposite outcome — the difference is whether the solution actually helps.

- **Pattern** — a proven fix for a real recurring problem, used where it fits.
- **Anti-pattern** — a common "solution" that looks reasonable but creates more problems than it solves (e.g. a God Object doing everything).
- A pattern applied to the wrong problem, or forced everywhere, **becomes** an anti-pattern in practice.

More in [anti-patterns-code-smells](anti-patterns-code-smells).

A pattern should **remove** complexity, not add ceremony.

- Start with the **simplest code** that works; reach for a pattern when a real, recurring pain shows up.
- Don't pre-build a Factory or Strategy for a class that will never have a second implementation.
- If a pattern needs three new classes to solve a problem a single `if` would fix, that's **over-engineering**.
- Name the pattern in code reviews and comments — that's the vocabulary payoff.

Common mistakes:

- **"More patterns = better design."** No — unnecessary patterns add indirection with no payoff.
- **"Memorize the 23 and you're done."** Interviewers care that you can spot *when* to use one, not recite the list.
- **"Patterns are language-specific tricks."** They're design ideas — the implementation varies by language, the intent doesn't.

blocks.subTitle: What is a design pattern?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a design pattern?**

A reusable, named solution to a design problem that recurs across projects. It's a template you adapt to your own classes — not a library you import and not copy-paste code.

blocks.subTitle: The three GoF categories
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Name the three GoF categories with an example each.**

**Creational** (object creation) — Singleton. **Structural** (composing objects) — Adapter. **Behavioral** (object interaction) — Observer. Give the category's job in one phrase, then a name — that's what interviewers listen for.

blocks.subTitle: Pattern vs anti-pattern
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How is an anti-pattern different from a pattern?**

A pattern is a proven fix used where it fits; an anti-pattern is a common approach that looks like a solution but backfires — like a God Object that takes on every responsibility. Even a real pattern becomes an anti-pattern if it's forced somewhere it doesn't belong.

blocks.subTitle: When not to use a pattern
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: When should you NOT use a design pattern?**

When the simple version already works and there's no real second case to support. Adding a Factory or Strategy for a class that will only ever have one implementation is over-engineering — it adds indirection with nothing to show for it.

blocks.subTitle: Talking about patterns in an interview
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How should you bring up patterns in a design interview?**

Name the pattern only after you've explained the problem it solves — "clients need to swap algorithms at runtime, so I'd use Strategy here" — not the reverse. Naming a pattern with no problem behind it reads as memorization, not design sense.

blocks.subTitle: Are all 23 patterns equally useful today?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Are all 23 GoF patterns equally relevant today?**

No. Some (Strategy, Observer, Factory Method, Decorator) show up constantly in real code and frameworks. Others (Interpreter, Flyweight) solve narrower problems you'll rarely hit directly. Know the common ones cold; recognize the rest by category.
